body_markdown:
Camaro vs. World is back. Finally. Summer was packed with diversions that kept delaying my project-car plans, kicking the old Chevy-shaped can down the road. Chief among them: my straight-laced day job, a full docket of freelance obligations,[a kid who’s all hopped up on monster trucks](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/kinardi-line/kinardi-line-9-what-monster-trucks-could-teach-formula-1/) , and a BMW-powered Corvette with a[penchant for grenading its own guts](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/kinardi-line/kinardi-line-11-failure-is-most-definitely-an-option/) .


But now, with race season well and truly over, the Camaro has elbowed its way back into my mechanical triage chart. First, however, I had to address some smaller items on my fleet punch list. After that, I could sort how to get the bigger, hairier[Camaro vs. World project](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/camaro-vs-world/) restarted.


In the period between buying parts to fix[the Ten-Dollar Miata](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/kinardi-line/kinardi-line-2-the-10-miata-ill-never-shake/) and installing them, the little Mazda roadster had become almost undrivable. Naturally, I waited until the exact moment I needed the car to address its problems.


I’d earmarked the Miata as my shuttle for driving up into the mountains, where the shop is located. I finally got the new clutch and flywheel installed, both of which I bought back in February. Momentum from the job also motivated me to tick a few more items off the laundry list: Fresh transmission, diff, and brake fluids went in, plus some stainless brake lines I’d been meaning to install since Covid…


To round off the job, I spent a few more shekels chasing a stuttering idle that had escalated to a misfire under load, plus some oil dripping off the back end of the head somewhere. A sooty fried spark plug on cylinder #3 and close inspection of the oil leak narrowed the fix down to a cam angle sensor (CAS) O-ring. I installed a new valve cover gasket as “while I’m in there” insurance.


For once, a three-year-old’s hands weren’t scattering these valve cover bolts into my wife’s flower beds.


Kyle Kinard


It was one of those rare, breezy jobs I could complete in the time my son was down for a nap. I found joy in the process of doing something—just one single gotdang thing—without interruption. The Mazda shop manual lay open near me more by habit than necessity, offering a decent outline of the procedure, but missing much of the granularity of the job. The removal of several brackets and even the location of the CAS itself went without mention.


As most Hagerty readers will know, fixing cars ain’t exactly building Legos, even if the fundamentals aren’t all that different on paper. Pull off old part, put on new. But fixing classic cars especially requires a degree of confidence in dealing with uncertainty, a base of experience that tells you when it’s time to close the book and trust what you know by now will actually work. Wisdom, in other words.


## As for the Camaro…


Last time we saw the Camaro, the engine was in and the suspension install was imminent. Life, and corrosion, called for a zag.


Kyle Kinard


Wisdom: It took a dose to decide that removing the old Camaro subframe and installing a new one was worth the hassle. It would prove to be a crucial step, though—a final hurdle that, once cleared, would allow our project to move forward at a clip for the first time in months.


After perusing Facebook Marketplace and rejecting a few used subframes that turned out to be[equally as crooked as our own](https://www.hagerty.com/media/our-garage/camaro-vs-world-6-fits-starts-oxidation/) , I threw a new subframe from Auto Metal Direct (AMD) onto the Visa card for the absolutely-not-a-bargain price of $1299. I suspect most of that cost was shipping the part from Taiwan and then humping it up the mountain to the shop, because a piece of precision engineering this AMD subframe is not.


For one, the subframe is a recreation of the F-body Camaro’s crude lump. A Swiss timepiece the original GM subframe is not. There are some slaggy welds down the length of the AMD subframe’s seams, which isn’t unheard of but is not exactly what you want to see on a four-figure part that’s holding the whole front half of your car together.


I can see the comments below this article in my mind’s eye already, telling me not to worry about it. You’re (probably) not wrong, dear readers. I’m just an anal-retentive, anxious fool.


You can’t call the AMD subframe gorgeous, but it sure as heck beats *this.*


Kyle Kinard


That said, the AMD subframe *is* built from thick-gauge steel. The powder coating looked flawless and held up to the dings of installation. The subframe’s stampings are sharp and neat, and most importantly, the unit proved to be arrow-straight.


In lieu of the actual locating pins for the subframe, we had a pair of bolts that fit absolutely perfectly into the locating holes, maybe 1/32 of an inch of clearance around the bolts’ outer diameter. Not to jump ahead too far, but with everything aligned and the subframe bolted up to the body, those locating bolts fell straight out of the center of their holes—a reassuring indicator that both the Camaro’s body and the subframe itself are squared.


Or at least as square as a Sixties pony car can be after all these years.


Originally, I wanted to shell out for one of the new tube-frame subframes you’ll find from the high-end restomod shops, but those cost thousands more and crucially don’t accept 15-inch wheels, owing to the C5 Corvette components and brakes run (nearly) across the board on those setups. Having now seen and installed this absolute unit from AMD instead, I’m at least confident the subframe will prove to be solid, robust, and long-lasting, if not beautiful or lightweight.


Kyle Kinard


Kyle Kinard


Darned solid, crude in places, and arrow-straight. AMD offers a decent like-for-like option for replacing that bent old subframe on your classic.


Kyle Kinard


Still, there were a few hiccups with the install, places where, like with the Miata, you had to lean on intuition or just plain git-er-done. The directions that came with the subframe confused matters as much as guiding them. Check it out:


The bushings/rubber bits to connect the body and subframe, and the printed directions on how to assemble the connectors. Somehow the photo looks about 50% clearer than the actual printout.


Kyle Kinard


Under the right light, we could just make out which rubber bushings, shells, and washers were meant for each of the six install points for the subframe. The diagrams weren’t very helpful at showing proper orientation of the bushings within the stack of parts. But the sheet did provide just enough direction and context for us to fill in the cracks ourselves and get everything assembled, aligned, and installed.


Only one piece of the subframe hardware kit required modification: A washer that was intended to sit between one of the bushings and the subframe couldn’t slot into place without contacting the subframe itself. After a trip to the bench vise and full attack with the angle grinder, we were back in business.


The offending washer.


Kyle Kinard


Further proof that an angle grinder and file can, and will, solve any problem.


Kyle Kinard


My other complaints about this aftermarket subframe are relatively minor, but I submit them here to offer room for welcome improvement. Instead of relying on a bolt that screws directly through the clips and into a threaded hole (or a welded nut on the inside of the subframe tubing), like on the original subframe, the AMD unit simply has blanks in the sheetmetal where the threaded holes should live, with no additional hardware to remedy the situation. We’ll use threadserts to attach the various clips that hold brake lines and other bits and bobs to the subframe itself.


Not a deal-breaker, but an inconvenience. We’ll find the appropriate-sized threadserts and keep truckin’.


The new subframe, installed and straight. After months of backtracking the build, the fresh small-block and Ridetech suspension can go in next. That first burnout isn’t so far away now.


Kyle Kinard


Besides the awkward fitment of one bushing washer, the install went smoothly. At least, until our transmission crossmember—which fit perfectly on the old subframe—simply would not mate up with the new AMD subframe *or* go back together the way we’d taken it off the old subframe. I don’t know how to explain it, but I can’t recall feeling more confused by a simpler part. The holes were simply… off. Had some unseen stress on the subframe put our crossmember out of alignment? I don’t know.


We ended up flipping one crossmember mounting bracket, and then using a ratchet strap to pull the trailing ends of the subframe together. That tiny bit of movement allowed us to install the hardware and bolt up the crossmember.


No biggie, but just baffling. And, again, not something you’ll find in the factory manual. There’s satisfaction in setting aside the literature and digging into your old bag of tricks to get the job done. A fairly standard-issue day in the shop, all told, made even sweeter by the Seahawks’ defense absolutely dunking on Patrick Mahomes in the background of our work.


Last step. When it came time to set final torque values for the subframe bolts, we reached for the period-correct shop manual, produced by Fisher Body in 1967. Of course, after flipping through the manual for 10 minutes, we couldn’t find any torque values for the subframe bolts. So I thought for a moment, set the torque wrench to 75 lb-ft, and got to turning.


We’ll check that again later. Seems like the wise move.


The *Body by Fisher* service manual. Gorgeous, nostalgic, and useless.


Kyle Kinard
